area_title: Cookies general theory / plain CookieOptions / SameSite-Secure-HttpOnly final pass
what_area_is_about: ASP.NET cookie surfaces: CookieAuthenticationOptions, CookieBuilder, CookieOptions, Response.Cookies.Append and UseCookiePolicy
how Set-Cookie response headers become Cookie request headers and how cookie attributes constrain browser behavior
important attributes: Name, Path, Domain, Expires/MaxAge, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, IsEssential and Priority
browser storage/devtools view, cookie persistence, normal cookie lifecycle and multiple cookie-name/scheme issues
general theory around first-party, third-party and partitioned cookies including CHIPS/Partitioned-style notes
HttpOnly vs non-HttpOnly storage, refresh-token notes and XSS/CSRF/security tradeoffs
SameSite Strict/Lax/None behavior, why SameSite=None requires Secure, and why CORS credentials do not override SameSite rules
HTTP vs HTTPS visibility: Secure controls whether cookie is sent over HTTP; HTTPS protects transport but not JavaScript access unless HttpOnly is set
key_ideas: Authentication cookie options and plain CookieOptions overlap in attributes, but they apply at different layers: auth ticket cookie vs arbitrary application cookie.
The browser enforces Set-Cookie attributes; the server emits them but cannot force the browser to send a cookie when SameSite/Secure/Domain/Path rules do not match.
Cookie.Name matters because multiple auth schemes or apps on the same host can collide when names/paths/domains are too broad.
HttpOnly hides cookie value from JavaScript but does not stop the browser from sending the cookie automatically with matching requests.
SameSite is mainly about cross-site request context, not about whether frontend CORS policy is configured correctly.
SameSite=None is the practical option for many cross-site cookie flows, but modern browsers require Secure with None.
Secure does not make a cookie unreadable to JavaScript; it only prevents sending it over plain HTTP and relies on HTTPS transport protection.
CORS credentials allow the browser to include credentials in an allowed cross-origin request, but SameSite may still prevent the cookie from being attached.
